SAN Francisco, November 27.--One
of the greatest trotting matches that
ever occurred of this coast, and one
which has been the subject of much in.
terest. t.all over the country, took place
at Bay District Park to-day. The at.
tendance was the largest seen here in
many years, estimated at nearly ten
thousand. There was heavy influx of
visitors from outside of the city, most of
the sporting fraternity all over the coast
being present. The weather was most
favorable, the sun shining brightly,
while not a breath of air was stirring.
The fair sex were present in goodly
numbers and were much interested in
the sport. The match was for purse

to the first horse, fifteen hundred to the
second and five hundred to the third.

Before the first heat Harry Wilkes was

and twenty dollars, Guy Wilkes bring.
ing fifty, and lrab, Hilton and Antevolo
comprising the field, selling for forty.
A good start was effected for the first
heat, Arab and Antevolo slightly lead
ing. They maintained the lead to the
quarter. when Harry Wilkes moved up
and was leading the procession by a
length at the half. When the three.
quarter post was reached, Harry had in
creased his lead to two lengths, while

ha MANLY farp,o with the

most certain that Harry would win and
there were no pools sold. After several

bad start in which Harry was three

A Good Way to Can Tomatoes Whole.-Select
nice, large, smooth tomatoes. Wash them and
put them in deep pan then cover with boiling
water and let them stand for five minutes. This
will loosen the skins. Pour off the water, and
pare the tomatoes. Now lay them in deep dish
and put them into moderately hot oven. Cook
for thirty minutes, being careful that they do not
get Drowned. When these tomatoes are put into
the oven, put stew-pan of sliced tomatoes on the
fire. Stir frequently to prevent burning. When
they have been stewed for twenty minutes, rub
them through fine strainer; then return to the
stewpan. Place some self-sealing cans on the
fire in pan of cold water, and heat the water
gradually to the boiling point. When the whole
tomatoes are done, take the dish from the oven
and transfer the tomatoes to the hot jars, being
careful not to break the vegetables. Pour the
juice into the jars and fill up with the strained to-
matoes, which must be boiling hot. Have the
jars SO full that little juice runs over. Now put
ON the elastic bands and covers Tighten the
covers as much as possible and when the jars be-
come cold, tighten the covers again. Place in
dark, cool place. In the Winter these tomatoes
can be used for salads again. For pack of the
whole tomatoes use two quarts OF sliced tomatoes
for the juice to fill the cans. In some cases this
will prove too much but what is left over may
be used for soup, sauce or catsup. ----

heated in water, and fill and seal as before.

This story, told originally by Spur
geon we believe, will, we are confident,
strike chord in many loving hearts:


A young clergyman and his bride
were invited guests at large party given
by wealthy parishioner. In all the
freshness and elegance of her bridal
wardrobe the young wife shone among
the throng, distinguished by her come
illness and vivacity and rich attire; and
when during the evening, her young
husband drew her aside and whispered
to her that she was the most beautiful
woman in all the company, and that his
heart was bursting with pride and love
for her, she thought herself the happiest
wife in the world. Ten years later the
same husband and wife were the guests
at the same house, where was gathered
a similar gay company. The wife of
ten years ago wore the same dress she
had worn on the previous occasion:
and, OF course, 1t had been altered and
re-made, and was old-fashioned and al
most shabby. Toll and care and moth
erhood and pinched circumstances had
taken the roses out of her cheeks and
the activity out of her form. She sat apart
from the crowd, care-worn and preoc-
cupied. Her small hands, roughened
with coarse toll, were ungloved, for the
minister's salary was painfully small. A
little apart the ten-year husband stood
and looked at his wife, and as he OBJ
served her faded dress and weary atti-
tude great sense of all her patient,
loving faithfulness came over his heart.
Looking up, she caught his earnest gaze,
and noticed that his eyes were filled
with tears. She rose and went to him,
her questioning eyes mutely asking for
an explanation of his emotion; and
when he tenderly took her hand, and,
placing it on his arm, led her away from
the crowd, and told her how he had
been thinking of her as she looked, ten
years before, when she was bride, and
how much more beautiful, for all her
shabby dress and roughened hands, and
how much he appreciated all her sacri-
flee and patient toll for him and their
children, great wave of happiness fill
ed her heart, light shone in her face
that gave it more than its youthful beau
ty, and in all the company there was
not so happy couple as this husband
and wife, their hearts and faces aglow
from the flaming up of pure sentiment
that transfgured and ennobled and
glorifed all the tolls and privations they
had endured.

sci. Counsel was appointed for him and
the cases were continued to this morn.
ing, when Clark pleaded guilty to the

upon pronounced judgment, giving him
fourteen years at San Quentin for the

Canned Fruits.-The American Grocer, a
prominent trade journal, has upon many occasions
placed before the people, through the medium of
its columns, much valuable information relative
to food authorizations, alleged poisonings through
which have received mention in its columns.
Recently it addressed letter to Lieutenant Gree
", of Polar exploration fame, asking him to give
his experiences relative to the effects of freezing
upon canned fruits and vegetables, especially as
regards the texture and flavor of tomatoes, corn
and other articles In reply, Lieutenant Greedy
states that apples pears, rhubarb, green peas,
green corn onions, potatoes and tomatoes were all
subjected to the extreme temperature of 60 degrees
below Zero and were of course solidly frozen.
During the second summer they thawed and then
froze solid again. After all this they presented
the same appearance as when freshly canned and
had as good favor as at the beginning They
were, however, irst-class goods. A few articles,
cranberry sauce and preserved damsons and
peaches, underwent some changes which detract
ed somewhat from their flavor, but not materially
so but this had been predicted by those who put
them up. Canned turnips. squash, beets, carrots,
pineapples, cherries, grapes, CLANS, shrimps and
crabs, although not subjected to such great ex-
tremes of temperature yet froze and thawed re-
peatedly without injury. No cans ever burst by
action of cold or heat except few fruit buffers.
Although canned fruits were very freely used by
Greely's men, no illness ever resulted therefrom,
and those using them were the strongest and
hardest of the party. These facts establish the
value and heathfulness of these foods under all
extremes of temperature.

Captain Walace's niece, a young English girl,
married a sea captain and went in his sailing
vessel with her husband, visiting many coun-
tries with him. On her first trip, when she
was yet young bride, there was a mutiny,
and her husband was wounded or knocked
senseless in his cabin. The sailors were about
to spring down the companion-way into the
cabin, when the young woman barred the way,
pistol in hand, and promised to shoot the first
man who moved toward her. She held them
thus at bay till wrath burned out, and the
mutiny was at an end. On the next voyage
they were shipwrecaed, and this brave-hearted
girl, with her young baby, was lashed to the
rigging. and remained there for several days
before they were rescued. They had nothing
to eat, and the mothers natural food for her
child was exhausted. BY some means a can OF
meat was lished up from the ship, aud the child
1ed on this until ii was ali gone, and the little
one about to starve But the mother put her
teeth into her hand, between the thumb and
1orefinger, and bit a cash into her own flesh,
from which the blood flowed. The child sucked
this, and that night the almost dying crew and
the brave Salor-wiTe were rescued.

BALDWIN, December oath, 1885.


Editors Baltimore County Union THAT per-
picking disease, hog cholera, has been more fatal
in Long Green Valley this year than last, and on
some farms, which were previously exempt, nearly
all the hogs have died. This is particularly the
case with o fine drove of full Berkshires-about
twenty five head-which has now but three left,
all the rest dying during the fall.


Your correspondent, who advocated in your
paper last year bran slop not only good, healthy
food, but ready preventive of the disease is con-
frmed in his appreciation of the remedy by the
treatment this year of the drove alluded to- for
two years previous bran slop was fed without the
loss of a hog while this year none was used. In
his own last year three hogs sick, which,
with the rest, were fed on bran slop during the
fall only and after the disease had become quite
fatal in the neighborhood, but they all recovered
and made fine hogs for late killing. This year,
with the germs supposed to be on the place, the
bran slop was fed earlier and not hog was sick,
and at the killing the livers and kidneys showed
unusually fine health, as there was not spot on
any of them. These hogs had the milk and house
Stops during the year and when the bran was fed
it was mixed with it, and in the fall ear corn was
added for fattening. They had not the advantage
of clean pen, as it was overlooked twice, and the
house part being old too rotten for repairing.
clean pen had certainly nothing to do with the
health of the hogs. G..

WILMINGToN, DEL, Jan. "a collision oc-

Last nights snow storm caused the most seri-

mington and Northern train, which leaves for

ton. Il consisted Of engine, baggage and mail

drifts the train was piloted by shifting engine.

progress was blocked by several freight cars
that had been thrown from the track by
near the gas house and there crossed to the
south bound trace, when IL again started for

Wilmington and Northern train was also under

HOllingsworth Co.'S tracks the engines and
train came together with q terrific crash. The
lain INTO tse baersee car teescopinS the ear

and the machinery twisted into all shapes

There is still ample room for advancement and

but of late there have been wonders accomplished

statement to the effect that an engine made speed

locomotives are now turned out of the works which

been neglected, and the old camel backs which
first drew heavy trains over the Alleghanies are
being supplanted by still more powerful Moguls.

increased demand for speed and power will come
the machines to meet it, perfect though the loco
motive Of to-day may now seem.

The little child, Anabel flanagan,
who recently went nearly two months
without food, is in this city to 'recov-
err" Last spring Anabel began to lose
appetite and gradually discarded the
use of food. At first she gave up tea
and coffee, then she stopped eating
meat and butter. Vegetables were
dropped next, and finally she even
stopped milk and fruit. During her
long fast she virtually lived on air and
water. She drank in great quantities
and inhaled the atmosphere with much
satisfaction. She became dreamy and
slightly preoccupied, but did not de-
cline in health, Her cheeks became
pale, but she was not reduced in weight
to any extent. by order of physician
she was regularly bathed in milk and
olive OIL She was also induced to take
minute homeopathic pills. Every device
was resorted to to stimulate taste for
food, but she rejected them all alike.
The tifty-third day she was seen to nib
bic a crust of bread. From that time
she commenced TO gradually recover
her appetite. She began with the same
things that she left of, but even now
she will not touch meat. During the
last fifty-three days she lost but ten
pounds, and even that may be due to
the fact that she was constantly har-
raised by the curious and inquisitive.
She now has rudy skin and shows
no symptoms of ill.health. The fact
that she suffered no pain nor inconven-
fence makes it hard to understand her
case.-St. Paul (Minn.) Special

A morning ride to Cotton on the Z

delicious indeed. The orchards of the
valley and the plains and hills are all
covered with flowers glistening with the
morning dew. The grand old noun
tains, in their white robes OF driven
snow. look down with patronizing air

chards, where the lark and liunet arc

while the new risen sun transtig-
ures the bridge of vapor into an
for half hundred miles these scenes
appear and change and reappear in
ravishing beauty, wrought out by the
early sunbeams.


At Cotton the scene changes, the pee-
Pile are too busy to look at the grain

hands, and the sound of Improvement is

The pecan tree freely resembles the
hickory, and the wood is very similar
and used for mechanical purposes as
hickory. The advantages for raising
pecans here rather than hickories are:


|. The pecan being Southern tree,
is adapted to sand here more than the
hickory.

taller tIee, will furnish greater amount
of choice commercial timber than the
hickory.


3. They are vastly more prolific than
hiekories, and never blight their crop
from intense heat, as hickories some
times do.


4. Being of taller growth they are
best adapted to form thick groves,
where their dense shade will do away
with all necessity for care and irriga-
tion.


Pecans are very prolific and profitable
and but little cultivation is required.

years from the seed if not transplanted.

Men, signing, say: "Our lives depart;


We cannot keep one precious day,


Though every slant, receding ray
Pierce like an arrow through the heart.
'sWith lettering pace our childhood went;


Like singing birds our youthful days


Flew swift beyond the yelling haze,
And soon will manhood's strength be spent"
Leaning on Him of old, who spake


Words that the centuries have told,


I, his disciple, will make bold
An echo of His truth to wake.
Within the soul power lives


To keep its life forevermore,


And walk rich laden to Heavens door
With all the wealth that earth-life gives.
But like riddle dim and strange


The words of hard condition read;


No life is won in very deed
Save by life lost in exchange.
Flowers yield their breath in gentle wise,


The great sun throws his glory down,


And neither fragrant flower nor sun
Could be, without the sacrifice.
Deep Human Heart, the secret read,


Lose and be evermore content


To see thy strength and sweetness spent;
Of them the dear Lords world hath need.
And when in sunset glory dying,

The day, this twilight world outlying.

Youths earnest love and burning zeal,


All good, that manhood's years reveal,

Brought loss of naught but night and death,

piece. The silver coins were excellent counter
feits, having the correct weight, the right Jingle

Spectacle.


The animal fights formed part Of tho

lation of the maharajah Of Cashmere.
Two huge water buifaloes, with ropes
on their feet. and dozen men Mt each
rope, were introduced to each other.
the crowd closing round them to with
in few feet. Neither animal requir-
ed any urging, but put his head down

opposing skulls rang like the sound of
Ratchet on wood across the arena
Then both brutes laid head to head and
pushed and grunted and paved and
swcatcd for five minutes, tho crowd
yelling madly meanwhile. The lighter
weight was forced back into the crowd,
recovered himself, butted again, turn
ed sideways. and was again forced
back. After few minutes more, when
each animal was settling down to his
work with whole-hearted earnestness,
the order was given to separate them,
and very reluctantly the gigantic mus
sucks were hauled in opposite direc-
tons.


Next came the fighting rams, spotted
and shaven beasts, with Roman noses
and rowdy visages, straining away
from their owners and all apparently
spelling for fight. Two or three coup
les were let 60 together, ran back to
gather way, came on, and met; ran
back, charged again, and repeated the
performance till the sound of their
foolish colliding heads was almost con-
tinuous. After the first few minutes,
when you begin to realize that neither
animal is likely to fall down dead, ram.
fighting is monotous. Sometimes
ram runs back to his charge valiantly
enough, and midway in the onset loses
heart, turns tail to his antagonist, and
fees to his master, The adversary be-
ing beast of humor, Immediately pulls
up and trots back to his master. One
light-limbed doomba with red spots
seems to be the campion of Jummu.
His charge GENERALLY upsets his an
tagonist at once, and few Of the rams
care to stand Il second.


As soon as all the rams had been dis
posed of, certain vicious shrieks and
squeals gave evidence that the horses
were being got ready, and the police
set about widening the ring. Presently
bay galloway and black pony dane
ed out, dragging their attendants after
them at the end of a long rope. The
instant they were let go they
ran open-mouthed at each other,
turned tail to tail, and kicked
savagcly for five minutes, the black suf-
fering most. Then, after the manner
of horses all the world over, they turn
ed round and closed, each striking with
his fore feet, and striving to fix his
teeth in the others crest They squealed
shrilly rs they boxed, and finally rose
on end-a magnificent sight, locked in
each others arms. The bay, losing his
hold on the blacks poll, made snatch
at the blacks near foreleg, which was
at once withdrawn.


Both horses then dropped to the
ground together, and kicked and bit at
close quarters till the bay fled with the
black after him through the crowd.
The saices at the end of the drag-ropes
were knocked over, scrambled up and
caught at the ropes again. while the
two maddcned brutes plunged and
struggled among the people. About
half dozen people were Knocked over
and shaken, but no one was hurt; and
after wild clamor and much running
hither and tbither, both bay and black
were caught, blindfolded, and led

The wife OF Jacob Freimuth, a home
steader in Seward county, Kansas, was
murdered and outraged by Fritz Rupin, a
half-witted German. Eupin had been Tor
some time enjoying the hospitality OF the
Freimuths. He was homeless and without
friends. and they had taken him in until
he could find work. During the tenn
porary absence OF Mr.. Freimuth, Rupin
overpowered his benefactor's wife and bru-
tally outraged her person and then killed
her. The posse then set out to scour the
country for the murderer, and found him
secreted in a small ravine, several miles
away from the scene of his crime, near the
Cinnamon river. A fractious and spirited
horse was secured and saddled. One end
of the long lariat was then fastened around
his neck and the other extremity
was attached to the pommel OF
the saddle. The horse was then started,
and amid the shouting of the men and
cracks OF rev volvers and rifles the frightened
animal tore madly away. After run OF
nearly five miles the beast fell exhausted
and the lifeless body OF the murderer was
loosened as soon as the men came up. The
lariat had drawn SO tight that his head
was almost severed from his body. The
features showed that he had died terrible
death. The body was feft on the prairie,
uncovered.

combustion among loose waste in the fire
room. The vessel was built in Bath,

dollars. When she took fire

destroyed. There was forty thousand
dollars insurance on the vessel. The
Mary and Helen was to have sailed to-
morrow on a sperm whaling cruise in
the South Pacific ocean.

Why need you care, dear wife, or heed
The passing OF your early grace?
What though the lilies supersede
The springtime roses of your face?
What though the azure of your eyes
Has mellowed to a softer blue?
The fairest tints that deck the skies
Are caught from twilight's fading hue.
Why should the ripened fruit regret
Its summer bloom, howe'er so fair?
Why need you sigh, though Time should set
His crown of silver on your hair?
The sweetest fragrance of the rose
Is from It's fading petals pressed.
Aud Nature spreads her earliest SHOWS
Above tine flowers she loved the best.
What care we for the vanished years,
Save for the fruit their summers brought?
What care we for our fallen tears,
Save for the rainbows on them wrought?
Why should we mourn the joys we shared,
Or see them perish with regret,
Since on the fruit our hearts have Jared,
And memory keeps the rainbows YETI
What though our winter time has come.
And summers buds and blooms expire?
Love hath an ever radient home,
And bids us welcome to the fire.
He dwelt with us through all the spring;
We sheltered him from summers heat;
Now at his hearth we'll sit and sing,
And let the wintry tempest beat.


LEE o. NORRIS.

The Pension Office investigation.
GEN. BLACK BELIEVES A PENSION WAS


GRANTED MARK ROBINSON ON POLITICAL


GROUNDS.


The Senate committee on public expendi-
lures to-day resumed the examination OF PEN
sion Commissioner Black. The case of Mark
Robinson, of Indiana, who was granted pen
sion in 1881, was taken up.


Gen Black said he believed the pension was
granted on political grounds. The papers
showed that Senator Harrison and Gov. Fos-
ter had urged the pension, and that the case be
made special and had set forth the political
services of Robinson. The case was made spec
ial and the pension allowed. Gen. Black said
that in his opinion the right to a pension was
never made out by the evidence; that fourteen
years after discharge from the armv the claim
for a pension was fled and no evidence cover
ing the claimants condition during these years
was presented. Gen. Black regarded the case
as one that was allowed through political favor
itism.


Adjourned until tomorrow.

LONDON, December 1.-The hearing Of


the Campbell divorce suit was resumed


to-day. Rosa Baer, formerly lady's maid


to the plaintiff, testified for the defense.


She said the Duke of Marlborough fre-

carriage in waiting. The carrisgs went

Witness often mailed letters to Chief

At this point COUNSEL for plainti6
cross-examined Miss Basr very closely

Being asked to explain how it came thai

Uncovered legs may compare oddly and more
favOrabiy to your brown, plump and bare

eral outcome every time. You are the old

votion, modesty and blunt truthfulness

impudent and precocious modern boy, with
modern ideas and habits, has crowded you out
of existence and taken the place you once SO
nobly adorned. The cows come home at milk
ing-time, but you, with your rawhide whip and
"bed-ticking" suspenders, are not there. You

There was once perfectly modern girl,
With perfectly modern ways,
Who saw perfection in everything


That happened to meet her gaze.
Such perfectly lovely things she said,
And perfectly awful, too,
That none would have dared to doubt her word,
So perfectly, perfectly true.
The weather, she said, in summer time,
Was perfectly awfully warm;
The winter was perfect, too, when there came
Some perfectly terrible storm.
She went to perfectly horried school,
In perfectly horrid town;
And the perfectly hateful teachers there
Did things up perfectly brown.
The lessons were perfectly fearfulIy long,
But never perfectly said;
And when she failed, as often she did,
Her face grew perfectly red.
The church she attended was perfectly mag
With perfectly heavenly spire,
And perfect crowds go there to hear
A perfectly charming choir.
The latest style is perfectly sweet,
The last the perfectest out
The books she reads are perfectly good.
(Just here we raise doubt.)
A ride she took was perfectly grand,
On perfectly gorgeous day,
With perfectly nobby friend of hers
Who happened to pass that way.
The perfectly elegant falls she'd seen
When on the way to the lake,
And the graphic description she gave us all
Was simply a modern mistake.
The perfectly splendid foam dashed up
In perfectly killing style,
And the perfectly terrible waves came down
In perfectly lovely pile.
I might go On with this perfect poem,
And write to the end of time;
But fearing to wear your patience out,
Will bring to an end my rhyme.

COLUMBUS, Neb., January i2.-The
news has just reached here from the
Dishner farm, some distance northeast,
that Minnie Dishner, the Nebraska
sleeping beauty, recovered conscious
ness on January 3rd, the sixty-seventh
day of her trance sleep. The roads
have been impossible until the present
time and news of her recovery could not
be received before. The girl fell into
the trance, from which she has now re-
covered, on October 9th, last. During
that long interval she has laid, TO all APP
D earances, a lifeless being, with the ex-
ception of respiration and pulsation.
When Miss Dishner awoke her mind
was apparently clear and unimpaired,
her appetite and general feelings good
but her arms and lower limbs paralyzed
She says that she was conscious during
the whole time OF her protracted trance.
but, although she sxerted her utmost
power to evince her CONSEQUENCES, she
could not move single muscle. She
says she had no physical pain, until the
fourth day of her sleep, when an electric
battery was applied. Since then she
has suffered thousand agonies OF body,
and, at times, it seemed as though her
mind would give way under the strain,
and she now complains Of terrible ply
sical suflierings, in consequence OF the
shock to her system. The doctor in at.
tendance says. however, that she will
recover In short time and will also re-
gain the use Of her limbs.
